title: ARGON: A GNN-Empowered Compilation Framework for Scalable Neutral Atom Computing
authors: Wenjie Sun, Xiaoyu Li, Zhigang Wang, Lianhui Yu, Geng Chen, Guowu Yang
abstract: Neutral atom quantum systems offer a promising pathway to large-scale quantum computing due to high qubit uniformity and flexible connectivity. To exploit this architecture, compilers must coordinate dynamic atom transport alongside highly parallel entangling gates. As circuits scale, the interplay between these operations becomes a system bottleneck, introducing denser logical interactions and longer temporal dependencies. Compilers must simultaneously satisfy rigid spatial constraints and complex movement schedules. Existing joint spatiotemporal compilation methods face an exponentially expanding search space, incurring substantial overheads or compromising fidelity as circuit size grows.   In this work, we propose ARGON, a scalable compilation framework that introduces a spatiotemporal decoupling paradigm for neutral atom processors. Our key novelty is offloading static geometric conflict resolution to an offline phase, precomputing a library of hardware-certified, high-parallelism spatial layouts. To guide temporal routing, we deploy a Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictor to evaluate candidate layouts against deep temporal horizons, proactively evading downstream kinematic bottlenecks. Finally, a heuristic router translates the selected sequence into collision-free physical transport.   Evaluations show ARGON completes compilation in under 10 seconds, delivering up to a >10^4x and 600x average speedup over state-of-the-art baselines. ARGON also minimizes routing decoherence and reduces Rydberg stages, improving execution fidelity by up to 10^2x on dense circuits.
summary: This paper introduces ARGON, a novel compilation framework designed to overcome the exponential complexity barrier in programming quantum circuits for neutral atom processors. By decoupling static spatial constraints from dynamic temporal scheduling using a GNN predictor, ARGON achieves massive speedups and significantly higher execution fidelity compared to current state-of-the-art methods.
main_problem: Compiling quantum circuits for neutral atom processors is bottlenecked by jointly optimizing dynamic atom transport scheduling and static spatial interference constraints, leading to an exponentially expanding search space.
main_result: ARGON achieves compilation in under 10 seconds, providing up to a $>10^4	imes$ speedup over state-of-the-art baselines while improving execution fidelity by up to $10^2	imes$.
method: The framework uses a spatiotemporal decoupling paradigm: precomputing static layouts offline and employing a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to predict viable temporal routes, which are then synthesized via heuristic routing.
model_or_system: The system is based on Neutral Atom (NA) quantum processors utilizing programmable optical tweezers for high qubit uniformity and flexible connectivity. Operations involve dynamic atom transport and entangling gates driven by the Rydberg blockade mechanism.
key_observables: Compilation Time, Physical Execution Fidelity, Average Speedup Factor.
important_parameters: Qubit Number ($N$), Interaction Radius ($R_{int}$), Decoherence rates.
main_assumptions: The core assumption addressed is that the joint spatiotemporal coupling can be broken by separating static geometric conflict resolution from dynamic temporal routing.

paper_structure: The paper introduces ARGON by identifying the joint optimization bottleneck, proposing a three-stage solution (offline layout library $ightarrow$ GNN prediction $ightarrow$ heuristic routing), and validating its superior scalability and fidelity improvement over existing methods.
why_interesting: It provides a critical software tool that directly addresses the scaling limitations of physical quantum hardware platforms like neutral atoms by abstracting away intractable combinatorial search problems into manageable, predictive inference tasks.

The compilation pipeline isolates spatiotemporal evaluations into three sequential phases: an offline spatial layout library construction, a GNN-guided predictive temporal placement, and a lightweight heuristic backend router. This decoupling effectively translates hardware-agnostic quantum circuits into collision-free physical transport trajectories.
